question: Where should we open our next facility, and what services should it offer?
caveat_blocks_removed: **C5. Facility counts must filter `ownership`.** Sacramento has 4 owned

detail.answer:
## Recommendation: a full-service acute hospital in Sacramento, CA

**Services:** surgery, cardiology, and an ER — in that order of value. Not oncology. Not more primary care.

### Why Sacramento

I ranked all 42 markets. Note first what *doesn't* work: `recapture_plan_paid_musd` ranks Atlanta and San Antonio on top, but recapture is a flat ~6.7% of allowed dollars in every market — it's just a market-size proxy, the C6 trap. Owned-dollar share is likewise 61–62% everywhere.

The measure that genuinely varies is acute access, and Sacramento is the worst market in the book:

| | Sacramento | Stockton | Modesto | typical market |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Active members | 52,420 | 31,840 | 21,909 | — |
| Median miles to owned acute | **75.0** | 48.9 | 53.2 | 7–17 |
| Acute care >30 mi from home | **95.7%** | 93.1% | 93.9% | 6–35% |
| Acute care in-market | **4.2%** | 5.1% | 2.6% | 53–69% |
| Owned hospitals | **0** | 0 | 0 | — |

Sacramento members' nearest owned hospital is in San Francisco — 75 miles. There are 10 owned facilities across this corridor and **every one is ambulatory-only** (`primary_care`, `imaging`, `labs`, `behavioral`). Zero owned surgery, cardiology, ER, or oncology within ~50 miles of 106,169 members.

I treated Sacramento–Stockton–Modesto as one catchment, per the dictionary's corridor guidance. Corridor-wide, 94,380 acute claims and **$348M in allowed spend** leave every year. But no single site covers it — the corridor is ~110 miles end to end, and the best possible placement reaches only 49.5% of members within 30 minutes. So build in Sacramento, which is both the largest block and the most stranded; Stockton/Modesto are a phase-two question, not a compromise mid-point.

### Which services

Sacramento's acute volume going out of market, by line:

| Service line | Claims/yr | Allowed | Recapture (plan-paid) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Surgery | 9,296 | $109.7M | **$9.36M** |
| Cardiology | 14,579 | $55.2M | **$4.74M** |
| ER | 27,704 | $28.7M | **$2.38M** |
| Oncology | 926 | $0.5M | $0.04M |

Surgery carries the economics, cardiology is second, and the ER earns its place on volume and as the admission funnel even though its own recapture is modest. **Oncology doesn't clear the bar** — 926 claims a year won't support a service line; keep referring it.

Equally important: **don't add ambulatory capacity.** In-corridor owned clinics already handle 256,060 of 299,297 ambulatory claims (86%). Primary care, labs, and behavioral are solved here. The gap is strictly acute.

**Sizing:** the eight owned hospitals cluster tightly at 11–21 ORs, 206–441 beds, ~10K OR cases each. Sacramento's out-of-market acute volume supports a peer-typical build — roughly 10–14 ORs and ~200 beds.

### What this is and isn't worth

Corridor-wide recapture from insourcing partner acute care is **$33.2M/yr** in plan-paid, repriced at the owned ratio (0.44 vs 0.624 partner, 0.80 out-of-network) per R6. Sacramento's own share is $16.5M/yr.

Two caveats worth stating plainly:

- A further **$107M/yr in plan-paid already flows to owned Bay Area hospitals** from this corridor. Bringing that home yields **no dollar savings** — the recapture figure on it is $0.09M. Its value is eliminating 66,355 claims' worth of 50–79 mile trips, and defending that volume against Sutter/UCSF/Dignity, who operate 12 hospitals inside the corridor today.
- Every owned hospital runs at only **51.7–54.6% OR utilization and ~55% bed occupancy**. The network is not capacity-constrained; it's geographically misplaced. This build is an access and retention case, not a capacity case — and it will cannibalize some SF, Fremont, and San Jose volume that already has room to spare.

One thing I couldn't size: the partner hospitals here all list obstetrics, but `obstetrics` doesn't exist in the claims service-line taxonomy (the eight lines are behavioral, cardiology, er, imaging, labs, oncology, primary_care, surgery). If OB is on the table for this facility, it needs a data source outside this warehouse.

## Recommendation: a full-service hospital in the Lodi–Galt corridor, between Sacramento and Stockton

**Services:** surgery, cardiology, ER, and imaging as the core. Not oncology.

---

### Where — and why not Sacramento proper

Ranking markets by `recapture_plan_paid_musd` puts Atlanta and San Antonio on top, but that column is almost perfectly linear in member count — it's a market-size proxy, and those markets already have hospitals with median 8–9 miles to acute care. It's not a siting signal.

The column that actually varies is access. Computing each California member's straight-line distance to the nearest **owned** hospital:

| City | Members | Avg mi to owned hospital | >30 mi |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sacramento | 50,639 | 75.0 | 50,639 |
| Stockton | 30,799 | 47.5 | 30,739 |
| Modesto | 21,148 | 51.6 | 21,122 |
| *everywhere else in NorCal* | ~340,000 | 4–25 | <2,100 |

**102,500 members are >30 miles from owned acute care, and 99.9% of them sit in these three cities.** Every other Northern California market is well covered.

A grid search for the single site covering the most of those 102,500 lands on a broad plateau around **38.25, −121.50** (Lodi/Galt):

| Candidate site | Underserved covered ≤30mi | ≤45mi |
|---|---|---|
| **Lodi/Galt (optimum)** | **78,550** | 84,743 |
| Elk Grove (S. Sacramento) | 58,444 | 82,795 |
| Sacramento city | 50,744 | 69,606 |
| Stockton city | 47,687 | 82,600 |
| Modesto city | 45,611 | 51,782 |

Siting in Sacramento city captures only its own 50.7K. The corridor site sits ~22 miles from both the Sacramento and Stockton member centroids and picks up **54% more underserved members**. This is exactly the multi-city catchment effect the data dictionary warns about — you cannot see it in per-city percentages.

Two supporting points: the optimum is a *plateau* (76.5K–78.5K across a wide area), so you have real latitude to site on land and labor-market grounds. And the corridor is uncontested — zero competitor facilities within 20 miles of the optimum, versus ~4,160 competitor beds within 20 miles of Elk Grove.

### What to build

Corridor demand, all 12 months, all ownership:

| Service line | Claims | Allowed $M | Recapture $M/yr |
|---|---|---|---|
| Surgery (acute) | 18,828 | 221.5 | **18.73** |
| Cardiology (acute) | 30,026 | 113.5 | **9.56** |
| Imaging | 78,202 | 60.0 | 5.04 |
| ER (acute) | 56,241 | 58.1 | 4.83 |
| Primary care | 210,900 | 38.3 | 3.22 |
| Labs / behavioral | 124,492 | 6.8 | 0.57 |
| **Oncology** | **1,860** | **0.9** | **0.08** |

Surgery and cardiology alone are **67% of both the dollar volume and the $42M/yr total recapture**. Skip oncology — 1,860 claims and $0.9M allowed across 102K members doesn't support a service line; keep referring it to San Francisco. Obstetrics appears in facility service-line strings but never as a claims service line, so I can't size it from this warehouse.

Sizing against your existing owned CA hospitals (1,007 beds and 57 ORs serving ~300K members within 30 miles) implies roughly **200–250 beds and 12–16 ORs** for 78.5K covered members — squarely in the range of your existing plants (207–345 beds, 11–21 ORs).

### Three things that should temper the business case

**The financial return is the $42M recapture, not the $499M of volume.** Most corridor spend already goes to *owned* facilities — Sacramento→San Francisco is 26,257 claims and $97.5M allowed; Stockton→Fremont is 15,357 claims and $56.0M. Moving that care from one owned hospital to another owned hospital saves nothing on the 0.44 `plan_paid`/`allowed` ratio. It buys travel relief and retention, not margin. Only the non-owned share reprices.

**This is not a capacity build.** Your four owned CA hospitals run 51.7–54.3% OR utilization and 54.1–55.2% bed occupancy. There is headroom; the problem is that the headroom is 75 miles from the members. Don't let anyone justify this on Bay Area congestion.

**One pattern deserves a sanity check before you commit capital.** Sacramento members are bypassing five local partner hospitals to drive ~75 miles to owned San Francisco. That is a strong latent demand signal for an owned corridor facility — but it's unusual enough that I'd want to confirm it reflects real plan steering rather than a facility-attribution artifact. If it's real, it's the single best argument for this build.

All distances above are straight-line haversine. The `external_drive_time_isochrones` table only covers existing facilities, so a real drive-time model for the corridor site is the obvious next step before you fix a location on the plateau.

## Recommendation: Sacramento, CA — a full acute hospital (surgery, cardiology, ER)

Then Stockton as phase 2. Here's what the data supports and what it doesn't.

### What I ruled out first

`market_summary.recapture_plan_paid_musd` is the obvious ranking column, and it's useless. It lands at **6.6–6.8% of allowed dollars in all 42 markets** — because partner share is uniform network-wide (caveat C6). Ranking on it just re-ranks market size and hands you Atlanta, which already has 11 owned facilities. Same for referrals: all 11 specialties in the corridor come in at ~11K referrals, ~22% with no in-network target, ~25% completed. No service-line signal.

### What actually varies: distance to owned acute care

I computed this independently of the mart, haversine from member coordinates to the nearest owned hospital:

| Market | Active members | Median mi | p90 mi | Owned hospitals |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sacramento** | 50,615 | **75.0** | 79.5 | 0 |
| **Modesto** | 21,136 | **51.5** | 56.2 | 0 |
| **Stockton** | 30,784 | **47.4** | 52.1 | 0 |
| San Jose | 97,828 | 4.8 | 10.0 | 1 |
| San Antonio | 119,863 | 5.2 | 10.6 | 1 |
| Atlanta | 122,473 | 7.5 | 12.3 | 1 |

Every other market is under ~13 miles. All four owned California hospitals sit in the Bay Area. The p90 tracks the median in the Valley, so this isn't a fringe of outlying members — the entire corridor is far.

The flows confirm the travel is real: Sacramento members consume **$106M** of acute care in San Francisco, Stockton members **$57M** in Fremont, Modesto members **$43M** in San Jose.

### Which services

Acute lines for corridor members, by share of spend staying in-market:

| Service line | Allowed | In-market |
|---|---|---|
| Surgery | $221.5M | **4.2%** |
| Cardiology | $113.5M | **4.1%** |
| ER | $58.1M | **4.1%** |
| Imaging | $60.0M | 62.8% |
| Primary care | $38.3M | 62.1% |
| Oncology | $0.9M | 3% |

The split is clean. The ten owned sites already in the corridor are all clinics and urgent cares offering exactly `primary_care, imaging, labs, behavioral` — and those lines retain ~62%. Everything acute leaves. **Build surgery, cardiology, ER. Skip oncology** — under $1M of corridor spend, it doesn't support a service line.

### Sizing

San Jose is the natural anchor: 97,828 active members served by one 244-bed, 11-OR hospital. Sacramento's 50,615 members scale to roughly **120–130 beds and 6 ORs**. Don't overbuild — the four existing CA hospitals run 51.7–54.3% OR utilization and ~55% bed occupancy, so the constraint being solved is geography, not capacity.

### Why Sacramento first, and why one facility isn't enough

No single site covers the corridor — median miles from each candidate:

| Site | Sacramento | Stockton | Modesto |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sacramento | 3.5 | 44.5 | 70.5 |
| Stockton | 44.6 | 3.5 | 27.3 |

Sacramento is both the largest single market (53.2K members within 3.5 miles) and the worst-served (75 mi). A later Stockton facility covers 32.3K locally plus Modesto's 22.3K at 27 miles — 54.6K combined, comparable to Sacramento. Modesto is never a first site.

### Two things to check before committing capital

**The ER numbers are not clinically credible.** Sacramento members show 27,704 ER claims with 4.2% in-market at a 75-mile median. Nobody drives 75 miles to an emergency room. The surgery and cardiology travel is plausible for planned care; the ER pattern suggests either a facility-attribution artifact in the claims or a geocoding issue. Validate against actual ED registrations before sizing the emergency department — it doesn't change the siting decision, but it changes the build.

**This is not a greenfield market.** Sacramento has 20 competitor hospitals with 4,554 beds; Stockton has 24 with 5,365. Members are traveling past available capacity because none of it is *owned*, not because none exists. That makes this a network-participation and steering problem as much as a construction problem — and it means volume ramp depends on contracting and referral redirection, not just opening the doors.

On the money: the acute partner→owned repricing across the three cities is **$33.2M/yr** in plan-paid. That's real, but as noted it's available at that same ~6.7% rate in any market. The differentiated return here is the 47–75 miles.
